paras: The lynching of J. H. Capps took place at Fort Fetterman, Albany County, Wyoming Territory, on the night of October 12, 1882, when a party of masked men took the cowboy from the post guard house and hanged him. Capps had been accused of shooting dead Richard P. Elgin, a bookkeeper for the cattle firm of Searight Bros., earlier that afternoon. Wyoming papers openly approved the hanging, and wire reports carried it nationally as the second lynching in the county within a short time.

Capps was a cowboy from Texas who had worked for Searight Bros. for about a year and, according to the Cheyenne Leader, had kept sober all summer. The papers do not state his race or that of anyone else involved. A Leader special said he had been drinking, had snapped his pistol at another cowboy, and had left camp saying he meant to kill somebody "to get even for the wrongs done him and get his name up."

At 3:30 p.m. on October 12, Capps was said to have shot Elgin as he stood at the counter of Altman & Webel's store, with no words exchanged between them. G. P. Searight, who was in the store, wrote that he saw Capps draw his revolver and that the second of two shots killed Elgin. Capps rode toward the Platte river bridge, fell from his horse, and on the bridge shot a cowboy, Michael Regan, in the groin when Regan refused to turn back.

Pursuers captured Capps and brought him back to the post guard house, where he was put in irons, and that evening a coroner's jury under Justice of the Peace J. D. O'Brien found that Elgin had died from a bullet fired by Capps.

About 11 o'clock that night, according to the Leader's correspondent, a party of masked men entered the guard house and ordered the guard to throw up his hands. They unscrewed the bolts of the cell, forced the door, dragged Capps out and hanged him to a beam of a high fence behind the guard house, where the body still hung at 9 a.m. A Cheyenne dispatch printed in Montana put the time at midnight and described the lynchers as a mob that overpowered the guard.

According to the Laramie Boomerang, as quoted by the Leader, Capps was cut down and buried on the second day after the lynching, and Elgin was also buried at Fetterman. Dr. J. W. Dysart of Laramie City, who attended Regan, judged his wound not fatal. No report of an inquest on Capps, or of any arrest of the lynchers, appears in the coverage.

The Cheyenne Daily Leader, which had its own correspondent at the post, headed its report "SPEEDY JUSTICE!" and opened with "Dick Elgin is avenged." Its local column said the hanging met "the approval of all lovers of justice even if Judge Lynch did conduct it," and a later item held that Capp "richly merited the fate that was so seasonably meted out to him."

The Laramie Boomerang went further in an editorial, "Hung by Request," which spoke of the county's "two hemp carnivals" and said it could not "come right out and condemn" them because each murder had been unprovoked. The editorial was reprinted as a western curiosity in the Arkansaw Traveler and the New York Dispatch on October 29.

Outside Wyoming the story ran as brief wire items, such as "LYNCHED BY COW BOYS" in Yankton and "Judge Lynch's Court" in Butte, from October 13 into late October in papers from Illinois to Kansas, Minnesota and New Hampshire. These condensed versions garbled names and places, printing Copp, Coop or Coppo for Capps, R. R. or R. H. for Elgin, and Egan, Eagan or Ryan for Regan, and several summaries placed the event at Fort Laramie.

A Boomerang dispatch carried by wire said the wounded man, "Mike Egan," joined a party of cowboys in taking Copp from custody, a version repeated in Kansas and New Hampshire. The Leader's local specials instead had Regan lying in critical condition at the hotel and named only masked men as the lynchers, which makes the Egan version doubtful.

bases: A party of masked men took J. H. Capps from the Fort Fetterman guard house and hanged him for the killing of Richard P. Elgin (A8, A22, A30).

Capps was hanged by 'a party of masked men' (A8) or 'a party of cow boys' (A1) who overpowered the guard, with no lawful authority, in revenge for the killing of Elgin, which the Cheyenne Leader called 'speedy justice' (A8, A7, A30).
Independent local specials to the Cheyenne Leader and the Omaha Bee and the Boomerang dispatch carried by wire agree that Capps was taken from custody and hanged (A8, A10, A4).

accounts.label: Eyewitness letter of G. P. Searight
accounts.gist: Searight saw Capp draw, heard two shots, the second killing Elgin; Capp was thrown from his horse and shot Regan on the bridge.

framing.detail: The Cheyenne Leader headed its report 'SPEEDY JUSTICE!', opened 'Dick Elgin is avenged', and later wrote that Capp 'richly merited' his fate.
The Laramie Boomerang's 'Hung by Request', reprinted in New York and Arkansas, said it could not 'come right out and condemn' the county's two lynchings.
Distant dailies and weeklies ran short wire items such as 'LYNCHED BY COW BOYS' and 'Judge Lynch's Court' without comment.

versions.value: A party of masked men; Regan lay wounded at the hotel

conflicts.note: The Leader's local specials, which place Regan in critical condition at the hotel, make his part in the lynching unlikely; the Boomerang wire version is the only one naming him.
The Fort Laramie version appears only in distant summaries; the local specials are datelined Fort Fetterman. 'Laramie City' is only the telegraph dateline (A1).
The Leader's on-the-spot special gives 11 p.m.
The later Boomerang report through the Leader says the doctor judged it not fatal.

record_check.dossier: The one person lynched was J. H. Capps (Copp is a spelling of the same man). Richard P. Elgin was the man Capps was accused of killing, not a lynching victim; 'F. Elgin' and 'J. D. Copp' do not appear.
Fort Fetterman; Laramie City is the telegraph dateline only.
Not stated in any article; Capps is described only as a cowboy from Texas.
A large party of masked men (local) or a party of cowboys (wire).

record_check.record: taken from custody by Egan and a party of cowboys
record_check.dossier: Only the Boomerang wire names Egan (Regan) among the lynchers; local specials have him lying wounded at the hotel and name only masked men.
Lynching: seizure from the guard house and hanging. The shooting was Capps's alleged act against Elgin and Regan, not the mob's.
